Key Research Thinking Patterns: Geometric Modeling: Uses geometric objects and actions on them to model and understand algebraic structures (like groups and operators) (e.g., using Bass-Serre trees to represent group splittings).

Invariant-Based Classification: Classifies mathematical objects by identifying crucial invariants or by reducing them to standardized minimal/canonical forms (e.g., using combinatorial invariants from triangulations to classify hyperbolic 3-manifolds).

Symmetry Exploitation: Utilizes group actions and symmetries as powerful tools to analyze structures, establish equivalences, and find canonical representatives (e.g. using PSL(2,ℝ) action to find canonical representatives for reflectionless systems).

Combinatorial-Geometric Translation: Translates problems between discrete, combinatorial settings and continuous, geometric/topological settings to leverage techniques from both areas (e.g. encoding surfaces into vectors to compute stable commutator length (scl) via linear programming).
Summary Description: Dr. Max Forester's research integrates Geometric Group Theory, Low-Dimensional Topology, and Spectral Theory, emphasizing the connection between algebraic structures and their geometric or combinatorial models. He investigates groups like generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups and lattices using actions on trees (Bass-Serre theory) and labeled graphs. In topology, he employs minimal ideal triangulations and spines to study hyperbolic 3-manifolds and their invariants, such as trace fields. His work includes analyzing stable commutator length via surfaces and linear programming. Furthermore, he connects operator theory with topology by examining reflectionless canonical systems, utilizing parametrizations and PSL(2,ℝ) actions. Forester's research often translates complex algebraic or analytic problems into tangible geometric/combinatorial frameworks to reveal underlying structures.
